title: Personality Prompts vs Plain-English Rules (Test Kit)
description: A controlled 180-reply protocol compares default prompting, explicit rules and the same rules plus an INTJ label. Includes tasks, rubrics and a worksheet.
h1: Do personality prompts beat plain-English preferences?
lede: Does telling an AI “Use an INTJ-style communication approach” add anything beyond plain-English rules? To find out, you have to hold the behavioral rules constant and test the label by itself. This kit gives you a 20-task, 180-reply blind protocol to run that exact test.
answer: This page provides an open test protocol (not completed results) comparing three conditions across 20 tasks and 3 repeats (180 replies): (1) Default, (2) Plain-English behavioral rules, and (3) those exact same rules plus 'Use an INTJ-style communication approach.'

sections.h2: The question this experiment can answer
sections.html:
Does adding the sentence “Use an INTJ-style communication approach” improve accuracy or usefulness compared with the exact same behavioral rules without the label?

Our earlier 60-reply pilot compared an untuned default against two full communication blocks (Straight answers and Thinking partner). This 180-reply protocol goes one step further by isolating whether the four-letter MBTI label itself adds value on top of plain-English rules.

1. Default: No added communication instructions.

2. Plain English:

Start with the answer or recommendation. Be concise and explicit about trade-offs. Correct false premises. State what is unknown instead of inventing facts. Follow the requested output format.

3. Personality label + the same rules: Prepend Use an INTJ-style communication approach. to the exact Plain English block above. Change nothing else.

Comparing Condition 1 vs Condition 2 measures the impact of the plain-English rules. Comparing Condition 2 vs Condition 3 isolates the effect of the INTJ label.

sections.h2: Freeze the tasks and run order
sections.html:
The downloadable kit includes 20 tasks across math, false premises, missing facts, editing, planning, data extraction, and formatting—each with a pass/fail correctness rubric. Running 3 repeats across all 3 conditions produces 180 replies.

Use a fresh chat session for every reply, keep model ID and sampling settings fixed, and follow the worksheet’s rotated condition order so position bias cancels out.

sections.h2: Blind the useful parts of scoring
sections.html:
Strip condition labels and give raters a shuffled sheet with opaque IDs, the task prompt, and the pass/fail rubric:

  • Primary outcome: Correctness pass/fail against the task rubric.
  • Secondary outcomes: Format compliance, usefulness (1–5 scale), and word count.
  • Usefulness anchors: 1 = unusable; 3 = usable after edits; 5 = ready to use and accurate.

sections.h2: Analyze paired tasks without inflating the sample
sections.html: Compare the three conditions within the same task and repeat. Report wins, losses, ties, and pass-rate gaps across all 20 tasks, and treat the 20 tasks (not the 180 total replies) as the primary unit when estimating uncertainty.
Download the 20 tasks and rubrics (JSON) and the 180-row scoring worksheet (CSV). You can also run quick side-by-side checks right in your browser with the Instruction Test Bench.
